Argot is a special, private vocabulary — a set of words, phrases, and expressions — used by a specific group of people, particularly to communicate among themselves in a way that outsiders cannot easily understand. Think of it as a group's secret linguistic code.

Imagine a gang of thieves in a city. They need to talk to each other about their plans, but they can't risk being understood by a passing police officer or a nosy stranger. So over time, they develop their own vocabulary. "The eagle" might mean the police. "Doing laundry" might mean hiding stolen money. "A warm jacket" might mean a weapon. This private, insider vocabulary — born out of a need for secrecy and shared only within the group — is their argot.

The word applies to any tight-knit group that develops its own insider language: criminals, prisoners, hackers, sailors, drug users, circus performers, soldiers, street gangs, and more.

Argot has a few defining qualities that set it apart:

It is group-specific. It belongs to one particular community or subculture. People outside that group won't know these words, or may hear them and mistake them for something else entirely — which is often the whole point.

It is functional and purposeful. Argot isn't just playful or casual language. It exists to serve a real need, most often secrecy, but also efficiency and group bonding.

It is intentionally exclusive. Unlike everyday language, which aims to be widely understood, argot aims to limit understanding to insiders only. Knowing the argot signals that you are "one of us." Not knowing it marks you as an outsider.

It is living and flexible. A group's argot can grow, shrink, and change over time. New words get added as new needs arise. Old ones get dropped, especially once outsiders start catching on.

Here are some real-world examples to make this vivid:

  • In old criminal underworlds, a "fence" meant a person who buys and secretly sells stolen goods — not a garden fence. A "mule" meant someone paid to carry drugs or contraband — not an animal. These were part of criminal argot.
  • In prison culture, a "shiv" is a homemade blade. The "yard" is the outdoor exercise area. New inmates had to learn this argot quickly just to navigate daily life.
  • Hackers have their own argot. A "n00b" (or "newbie") is an inexperienced person. "Pwned" means thoroughly defeated or taken over. To "script kiddie" someone is to insult them by calling them an amateur who just copies others' code.
  • Street drug culture has long had argot: "scoring" means buying drugs, "clean" means sober, "going cold turkey" originally meant the raw, unplanned process of quitting drugs suddenly.
How argot is different from similar words

This is where many learners get confused, so let's be precise.

Argot vs. Slang: Slang is informal, casual language used loosely across many groups and generations — words like "cool," "vibe," or "dude." Slang is not secret; anyone can pick it up from pop culture. Argot, on the other hand, is more exclusive, more deliberate, and more tightly guarded within a specific community. All argot starts as a kind of slang, but not all slang is argot.

Argot vs. Jargon: Jargon is the technical vocabulary of a profession — doctors talk about "myocardial infarctions," lawyers talk about "tort liability," engineers talk about "load-bearing tolerances." Jargon is specialized, yes, but it isn't meant to hide information — it's just efficient shorthand among experts. Argot, by contrast, carries an element of deliberate exclusion and often secrecy. A surgeon using jargon in an operating room isn't trying to confuse you — a criminal using argot on the street probably is.

Argot vs. Dialect: A dialect is a regional variation of a whole language — the way people in one city or country speak differently from those in another. Argot is not about geography; it's about group membership and social identity.

The reasons are layered and fascinating:

Survival and protection — This is the original driver for most criminal and marginalized groups. If the police, the enemy, or an authority figure can't understand what you're saying, you stay safe.

Identity and belonging — Speaking a group's argot is like wearing a uniform. It signals that you are truly part of the community. It builds trust. When someone uses the right word in the right context, it says: "I am one of you."

Efficiency — Sometimes a single argot word captures a complex concept that would take many words to describe in standard language. Insiders communicate faster.

Solidarity — Shared language creates a shared world. It strengthens the bond between group members and reinforces the invisible boundary between the in-group and the out-group.
What happens when argot "leaks" into everyday language?

This is one of the most interesting things about argot — it doesn't always stay secret. When a group's private vocabulary slowly becomes familiar to the general public, those words "leak" out of the argot and enter mainstream language. At that point, they usually lose their power as secret code, because the secrecy is gone.

For example: "Cool" as a slang term for something admirable originally circulated in African-American jazz communities in the 1930s–40s as part of that subculture's insider language. Over decades, it leaked into mainstream culture and is now universal. The same has happened with words like "hip," "bling," "hustle," "bread" (money), and many others. Once they're everywhere, they're no longer argot — they're just slang or even standard English.
Using the word "argot" correctly in a sentence

• "The detectives struggled to follow the suspects' conversation because they spoke entirely in their criminal argot."
  • "Every subculture eventually develops its own argot, a linguistic fingerprint that marks who belongs and who doesn't."
  • "She had spent years in the industry and was fluent in the argot of underground hip-hop."
  • "What was once the argot of street gangs has now become mainstream slang used by teenagers worldwide."

Argot is the private, insider vocabulary of a specific social group — most often used to communicate secretly, signal membership, and exclude outsiders — which can range from criminal underworlds to hacker communities to any tight-knit subculture with its own linguistic identity.
